item.title: Meth is a key driver in Fiji's fast-growing HIV epidemic: 1 in 60 adults are affected
item.description: In mid-September, Fiji's government declared a national emergency because of a startling rise in HIV infections. The country's crystal meth epidemic is a strong contributing factor.
item.content:encoded:
In mid-September, Fiji's government declared a national emergency because of a startling rise in HIV infections. The country's crystal meth epidemic is a strong contributing factor.

(Image credit: Ian Cheibub for NPR)

item.title: Meal deliveries can save money and improve health. Will they survive Medicaid cuts?
item.description: Some states deliver meals to Medicaid patients that address their dietary needs. Evidence shows it aids recovery and saves healthcare costs, but federal budget cuts may lead some states to cancel it.
item.content:encoded:

item.title: The U.S. has more thalidomide survivors than the government admits
item.description: In the 1950s and 1960s, doctors gave the drug thalidomide to pregnant patients without telling them — and without FDA approval. Now those patients' children want recognition.
item.content:encoded:

item.title: There's a global pandemic treaty that's signed -- and in 'limbo.' What's the holdup?
item.description: The treaty aims to help the countries of the world prepare for — and defeat — any future pandemic. Why hasn't it gone into effect?

item.title: Mom! Mom! MOM! 3 ways to stay calm in stressful parenting moments
item.description: Parenthood can be overwhelming. A therapist and mom of three shares techniques to help calibrate your emotions — so you can show up better for yourself and your family.

item.title: President Trump's FDA commissioner nom, Dr. Heidi Overton, faces Senators' questions
item.description: Dr. Heidi Overton has been nominated to be the new FDA commissioner. The Senate HELP committee pressed her on vaccines, mifepristone, food safety and whether she can tell the president he's wrong.

item.title: How to limit rat numbers? Train humans
item.description: No matter how much poison you put out, rats continue to thrive. So D.C.'s Rat Rangers are trying education (of people, not the rats). They take residents into back alleys to illuminate the problem.
